thread.title: Malaysia 10-Year Passport Fee: RM350 (2024 Update)

author: Lucas Fernandez - World Editor
title: Malaysia 10-Year Passport Fee: RM350 (2024 Update)
text:
Malaysia’s government has officially gazetted a new passport fee structure effective June 4, 2026, raising the cost of a 10-year international passport to RM350—a 75% increase from the previous RM200 fee. The change, announced by His Majesty the Yang Di-Pertuan Agong, applies uniformly across all Malaysian citizens aged 13–59, with concessions for senior citizens, children, and students. This policy shift, implemented under Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s administration, marks the first significant overhaul of passport fees in over a decade and carries broad implications for travel affordability, diplomatic relations, and economic mobility.
Why This Matters: The Cost of Mobility in a Globalized World The RM350 fee is not merely an administrative adjustment—it’s a financial barrier for millions. Malaysia’s passport is a gateway to 190+ visa-free or visa-on-arrival destinations, but the new cost could disproportionately affect low-income households, students, and rural populations. For context, the average monthly income in Malaysia’s bottom 40% bracket is RM1,500—meaning the passport fee now represents nearly a quarter of their monthly earnings. This isn’t just about travel; it’s about economic participation in an era where digital nomadism and cross-border work are increasingly vital.
Key Problem: The fee hike risks deepening inequality in mobility, potentially leaving vulnerable groups stranded in a world where borders are closing faster than visas are opening.
The Policy Context: A Decade of Stagnation and Sudden Change Passport fees in Malaysia have remained static since 2013, when the government last adjusted the RM200 rate for a 5-year validity. The shift to 10-year validity—aligned with global standards like the U.S. And EU—was framed as a cost-saving measure for frequent travelers. However, the fee increase outpaces inflation (which averaged 2.5% annually since 2020) and contradicts Malaysia’s push to attract foreign investment and talent through easier mobility policies.
Malaysian passport RM350 fee official poster “This fee hike sends mixed signals. On one hand, it aligns with global passport standards, but on the other, it penalizes the very citizens we need to remain globally connected—our youth, our workers, and our entrepreneurs.”
Datuk Seri Dr. Zeti Akhtar Aziz , Former Governor of Bank Negara Malaysia and Senior Fellow at the Institute of Strategic and International Studies (ISIS) Malaysia Regional Impact: Who Pays the Price? The fee increase will hit different communities unevenly:
Malaysian Rural Sabah and Sarawak: Where median incomes are 20% lower than Peninsular Malaysia, the RM350 fee could deter families from renewing passports, limiting access to medical tourism (a RM12 billion annual industry) and remittances from overseas workers. Kuala Lumpur and Penang: Urban centers with higher disposable incomes will absorb the cost more easily, but minor businesses relying on cross-border trade may face higher operational costs. Students and Young Professionals: The RM100 concession for students studying abroad remains, but the base fee now exceeds the monthly stipend for many scholarship recipients. Economic Ripple Effects: Beyond the Passport Office The fee hike intersects with three critical sectors:
Tourism and Remittances: Malaysia’s tourism sector contributes RM70 billion annually, with 25% of visitors arriving via visa-free routes. Higher passport costs for Malaysian expatriates could reduce remittances (currently RM110 billion yearly) if workers delay renewals. Diplomatic Relations: The fee increase may prompt reciprocal actions from neighboring countries. Indonesia, for example, charges USD $36 for a 10-year passport—less than Malaysia’s RM350 (≈USD $78). A fee war could emerge, complicating ASEAN mobility initiatives. Digital Nomad Economy: Malaysia’s “Digital Nomad Visa” program, launched in 2024, relies on Malaysian professionals working remotely abroad. The higher passport cost could discourage participation in this RM5 billion annual sector. Legal and Administrative Challenges The gazettement process was swift, but implementation raises questions:
Immigration Department postpones rollout of new Malaysian passport Backlog Risks: Immigration Department data shows a 30% increase in passport applications since 2025. Delays could occur if infrastructure isn’t scaled to handle the fee-driven surge. Concession Loopholes: The RM100 student fee requires proof of enrollment abroad. Without clear guidelines, many eligible applicants may face rejections. Legal Recourse: Citizens unhappy with the fee hike could challenge it under Article 12(4) of the Federal Constitution, which guarantees equal protection. However, past cases (e.g., Malaysian courts’ deferential stance to executive economic policies ) suggest legal victories may be slim. Solutions in the Directory: Navigating the New Reality For those affected, the path forward isn’t just about paying the fee—it’s about mitigating the broader impact. Here’s how professionals in our directory can help:
Malaysia Immigration Department passport fee 2024 announcement Financial Planning: Citizens facing hardship can consult certified financial planners to spread the cost over time or explore government aid programs like Bank Negara Malaysia’s financial inclusion initiatives . Legal Aid: Those seeking to challenge the fee hike may need pro bono constitutional lawyers specializing in economic rights cases. Organizations like Suhakam (Human Rights Commission of Malaysia) can provide guidance on constitutional grounds. Travel Optimization: Businesses and individuals can partner with visa and passport consultancies to strategize around the new fees, such as leveraging multiple-entry visas or regional travel passes. The Bigger Picture: A Test for Malaysia’s Global Ambitions This fee hike occurs as Malaysia positions itself as a regional hub for trade and talent under its National Investment Aspirations (NIA) 2030 plan. The contradiction is stark: while the government courts foreign investors with tax incentives and infrastructure projects, it raises barriers for its own citizens to move freely. The long-term risk? A brain drain of skilled workers who can no longer afford the mobility required to compete globally.
“A passport is more than a document—it’s a social contract between the state and its citizens. When that contract becomes unaffordable, trust erodes. Malaysia’s leaders must ask: Do we want a passport that’s a privilege or a right?”
Professor Shamsul A.B. , Dean of the Faculty of Economics and Administration, University of Malaya Looking Ahead: What’s Next? Monitor these developments in the coming months:
Will neighboring countries like Singapore or Thailand respond with retaliatory fee hikes? Will the Immigration Department introduce installment plans or subsidies for low-income applicants? Could this policy spark broader debates on citizenship costs, such as mandatory national service fees or digital identity charges? The RM350 passport isn’t just a price tag—it’s a litmus test for Malaysia’s commitment to its people in an interconnected world.
